principles.rule: Boring is the alpha — stack small sure-thing gains to beat your checking account
principles.rationale: Near-certain markets resolving tonight can return 1-4% in a single day, which annualizes far above a savings account. The key is stacking these 'bonding' plays repeatedly rather than chasing flashy long-shots.

citations.quote: Some of the best financial decisions you make are boring. Warren Buffett is like a really boring guy. He's doing it the boring way and that's his charm.
If you can get four percent in a day, it's pretty good.
You can stack those gains over a year if you're doing that once a week — kind of looks a lot better than a checking account, doesn't it?

principles.rule: Use the bonding play: buy near-certainties resolving today, not months from now
principles.rationale: The 'bonding' mechanism lets you step in at 96-99% and take the last 1-4% from holders who want liquidity. A 4% return in one evening is real yield, but only works because the event is imminent — don't apply it to races that resolve in November.

citations.quote: One of the terms you'll hear used in prediction market talk is called bonding — basically people will invest in something early on, it will go up to 98-99 percent when it's sure that it's going to happen, and people who have those positions want access to that cash. So they will sell out at 99 and a lot of people will say, this is a sure thing, I'm happy to come in at 99 and take that 1 off your hands.
A lot of times the smarter play is to keep it on the sidelines and pop it into races like this, where you are in a sure-thing environment.

principles.rule: Scan related markets for the best-value expression of the same thesis
principles.rationale: Multiple markets often price the same underlying conviction differently. The under-50% NO for Vivek offered better odds than betting he wins outright, because the market mispriced that outcome. Always shop across related contracts before entering.

citations.quote: Now one interesting thing — this is something that you'll learn looking around these markets — there is a position for Vivek Ramaswamy to win under 50 percent. The bottom line is there's more value in his under-50 percent — to say no, he won't be under 50 — than in whether he will win. I think there's almost no chance he's going to be under 50 percent.
A lot of times you can look around and find multiple markets looking at the same thing and find a slightly better advantage there than in other places.

principles.rule: Hedge your life — a position where losing money means a good outcome for you is worth a bonus
principles.rationale: When your directional opinion on a market coincides with wanting the other outcome to happen in real life, that overlap is a valid extra reason to take the trade. It is not the primary reason to enter, but it tilts the personal calculus in your favor.

citations.quote: One thing I love when it comes to prediction markets is when my opinion, my vibe, my position on a market coincides with me being able to hedge my life. Hedge my life is a very central part of my life — you'll hear it a million times here on Predictable.

The other thing I like about this — just to give me a little added push — is the fact that if I'm wrong and I lose this money, we've ended a war, and I'm going to be pretty happy about a war being over. So there's a little bit of a hedging-your-life thing there.

principles.rule: Read the resolution rules before sizing — 'permanent peace deal' is a much higher bar than a ceasefire
principles.rationale: Markets can resolve on announcements that feel like victory but don't legally satisfy the contract. Always read the resolution criteria; a 37% priced market might be even more mispriced once you understand exactly what triggers a YES.

citations.quote: I want to read those rules specifically to see what ticks that off, because you never know — sometimes it's just people saying they've got a permanent peace deal and that will check the box. This isn't a standoff where we all just say we won and people stop firing. We're talking about a permanent peace deal.
